paragraphs: Problems involving permutations require choosing an ordering or assignment of objects, which can make optimization difficult. This paper builds continuous relaxations using sorting networks. Its formulation is more compact than an alternative based on the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices, and requires only box constraints: upper and lower bounds on individual variables.

The authors apply this construction to the quadratic assignment problem and develop a coordinate descent algorithm. One cycle costs O(n² log² n), compared with O(n³) per iteration for the conditional-gradient method used by Fast Approximate QAP. These are different units of algorithmic progress, but they describe the computational work required by the respective update procedures.

Experiments show that a continuation method can work effectively with the new formulation. On most QAPLIB problems and a class of synthetic problems, the resulting solutions are competitive with Fast Approximate QAP, often requiring substantially less computing time. The contribution combines a simpler constraint structure with evidence of practical computational savings.
icml-2016-a-box-constrained-approach-for.tldr: Sorting-network relaxations simplify permutation optimization and often find competitive quadratic-assignment solutions in less computing time.

paragraphs: The paper studies objectives formed by adding finitely many convex functions, with the additional assumption that their sum is strongly convex. Standard incremental or stochastic methods for this setting have convergence rates that are at most linear. The authors seek faster convergence while retaining the incremental idea of updating only part of the optimization machinery at each iteration.

Their Newton-type incremental method, NIM, maintains a model of the objective that preserves its sum-of-functions structure. Each iteration updates a single component of that model. This construction brings Newton-type optimization into an incremental method, connecting information about individual component functions to progress on the overall objective.

The analysis establishes linear global convergence and superlinear local convergence. The distinction matters: the stronger rate applies near the solution, rather than throughout the entire optimization process. Experiments find the method particularly effective when there are many component functions but relatively few variables. That reported setting identifies where the proposed combination of incremental updates and faster local convergence is practically promising.
icml-2016-a-superlinearly-convergent-pro.tldr: NIM updates one objective-model component per iteration and achieves linear global convergence with superlinear convergence near the solution.

paragraphs: Deep generative models must support both generating observations and inferring the hidden explanations behind observations. A common approach pairs a top-down generative model with a bottom-up network for approximate inference. This paper changes how those two directions define the model, motivated by the connection between inference quality and the quality of learned generative models.

The bidirectional Helmholtz machine treats both directed networks as approximate inference distributions. The model distribution is defined through their geometric mean. This construction guarantees efficient inversion between the top-down and bottom-up distributions. The authors also derive a lower bound on likelihood that provides an objective for training the resulting model.

Optimizing that bound regularizes the two distributions toward agreement by minimizing their Bhattacharyya distance, a measure of distributional separation. The reported results include state-of-the-art generative performance, a preference for substantially deeper architectures, and likelihood estimation that is orders of magnitude more efficient. The central contribution is to make agreement between the two inference directions part of the generative model itself.
icml-2016-bidirectional-helmholtz-machin.tldr: Bidirectional Helmholtz machines combine top-down and bottom-up distributions through a geometric mean, improving generative modeling and likelihood-estimation efficiency.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification assigns an object a set of labels rather than a single category. Labels can depend on one another, so predicting each independently can miss useful structure. This paper proposes Conditional Bernoulli Mixtures as a way to capture those dependencies while reducing learning to several familiar binary and multiclass classification problems.

The framework includes both independent binary prediction and prediction over complete label subsets as special cases. This gives it a common formulation for approaches that otherwise treat label relationships quite differently. The authors implement the method with logistic regression and gradient boosted trees, using an Expectation Maximization procedure to train the mixture.

Prediction uses dynamic programming to avoid examining an exponential number of possible label sets. That computational step matters because the number of subsets grows rapidly as more candidate labels are introduced. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effectiveness against competitive alternatives, with advantages in accuracy, computational complexity, or both. The claim therefore concerns a useful combination of dependency modeling and efficient prediction, without asserting that every advantage occurs in every comparison.
icml-2016-conditional-bernoulli-mixtures.tldr: Conditional Bernoulli Mixtures capture label dependencies and use dynamic programming for efficient prediction over label sets.

paragraphs: The Ladder Network performs well in semi-supervised learning, where training combines labeled and unlabeled examples, but its intertwined components make the reasons for that success unclear. This paper investigates those reasons experimentally. The authors replace or remove individual components and compare the resulting variants to assess which parts contribute most.

For semi-supervised tasks, lateral connections make the largest contribution, followed by noise injection and the choice of combinator function. The relative importance changes as more labeled examples become available. Lateral connections and the reconstruction criterion become less important, while noise introduced at every layer accounts for most of the improvement in generalization.

The investigation also produces a new combinator function. On Permutation-Invariant MNIST, it achieves test error rates of 0.57% with supervised training, 0.97% with 1,000 labeled examples, and 1.0% with 100 labeled examples. These findings connect architectural choices to the amount of supervision available, while showing that examining individual components can lead to a concrete improvement in the complete network.
icml-2016-deconstructing-the-ladder-netw.tldr: Component-removal experiments identify what drives Ladder Network performance and yield an improved combinator function.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a service can estimate the distribution of a categorical statistic without collecting users’ underlying data. The target is an aggregate description, such as how frequently different categories occur. Local privacy constrains the information available for that estimation, creating a tradeoff between protecting individual data and retaining useful population-level information.

The authors introduce new mechanisms, including hashed k-ary Randomized Response. Their empirical results show utility that matches or exceeds existing mechanisms across all privacy levels considered. This addresses the practical side of the problem: whether privacy-preserving collection still provides enough information to estimate the categorical distribution effectively.

The theoretical results establish order-optimality for k-ary Randomized Response and the existing RAPPOR mechanism in different privacy regimes. Order-optimality concerns the scaling of estimation performance, rather than an assertion that every numerical detail is best possible. Together, the results show why privacy strength matters when choosing a mechanism: the theoretical justification for different methods applies in different regimes, alongside the empirical gains from the proposed mechanisms.
icml-2016-discrete-distribution-estimati.tldr: New locally private mechanisms improve categorical-distribution estimation, with optimal scaling guarantees for different mechanisms in different privacy regimes.

paragraphs: Dynamic Capacity Networks address how a neural network distributes computation across an input. Different portions may benefit from different amounts of processing, so the architecture combines low-capacity and high-capacity subnetworks. The smaller subnetworks operate over most of the input and help decide where the larger subnetworks should be applied.

The selection mechanism uses gradients to identify regions where the network’s output is most sensitive to the input. It then allocates additional capacity to a few selected regions. This makes attention a way to direct computation: the initial processing both contributes to the prediction and guides where more expensive processing should occur.

Experiments on Cluttered MNIST and SVHN indicate that this adaptive allocation can drastically reduce computation compared with traditional convolutional neural networks while maintaining similar or better performance. The finding is empirical and tied to those evaluations. Its significance is that substantial computational savings can come from choosing where to use capacity within an input, rather than applying the same amount of processing everywhere.
icml-2016-dynamic-capacity-networks-f8f1.tldr: Dynamic Capacity Networks use gradient-based attention to concentrate expensive processing on selected input regions, reducing computation in image experiments.

paragraphs: Dynamic memory networks use memory and attention mechanisms to support question answering. Earlier results showed strong performance on language tasks, but left two questions open: whether the architecture could perform strongly without training annotations identifying supporting facts, and whether it could handle questions about images. This paper addresses both questions through changes to the architecture.

The authors analyze the existing network and improve its memory and input modules. They also introduce an image input module, allowing visual information to enter the question-answering system. The resulting model, DMN+, extends the architecture’s scope while revising the components responsible for receiving information and using memory.

DMN+ improves the state of the art on the Visual Question Answering dataset and the bAbI-10k text question-answering dataset without supporting-fact supervision. This matters because the training process does not require explicit markings of the facts needed to answer each question. The results support the revised architecture across both visual and textual tasks, with the claim grounded in these two benchmark evaluations.
icml-2016-dynamic-memory-networks-for-vi.tldr: DMN+ improves memory and input processing to advance visual and textual question answering without supporting-fact supervision.

paragraphs: The large-scale distribution of matter carries information about cosmological parameters describing the Universe. A common approach summarizes galaxy locations with a function of scale, such as a correlation function or power spectrum. This paper investigates whether machine learning can estimate cosmological parameters directly from the distribution of matter.

The authors apply deep three-dimensional convolutional networks to volumetric representations of dark matter simulations. They also evaluate a distribution regression framework. These approaches make the matter distribution itself the basis for parameter estimation, exploring a different route from inference built around the conventional summarized representation of large-scale structure.

The reported machine learning results are comparable to maximum-likelihood point estimates obtained using cosmological models and sometimes outperform them. The evidence therefore supports direct estimation as a viable approach in the simulation setting studied, without claiming a universal advantage. The broader implication is the possibility of more accurate cosmological parameter estimation by developing methods that work directly with the spatial distribution of matter.
icml-2016-estimating-cosmological-parame.tldr: Machine learning applied directly to simulated dark matter distributions can match and sometimes outperform cosmological-model maximum-likelihood estimates.

paragraphs: Structured prediction becomes difficult when training provides indirect information about outputs instead of the outputs themselves. Maximum marginal likelihood then faces two obstacles: its objective can be nonconvex, and even computing one gradient can be intractable. This paper develops an alternative for a particular class of problems whose indirect supervision has a linear structure.

The method separates estimation into two stages. First, it solves a linear system to estimate the model’s sufficient statistics, the quantities used for the subsequent parameter estimation. It then estimates parameters through convex optimization. This sequence bypasses both computational obstacles for the supported class of linear indirectly supervised problems.

The authors analyze the statistical properties of the approach and evaluate it in two settings: learning under local privacy constraints and learning from inexpensive count-based annotations. The empirical results show effectiveness in both. The contribution is a concrete route from indirect observations to model parameters, where the linear relationship makes it possible to replace a difficult marginal-likelihood calculation with more manageable estimation steps.
icml-2016-estimation-from-indirect-super.tldr: For a class of indirectly supervised problems, linear-system estimation followed by convex optimization avoids difficult marginal-likelihood computations.

paragraphs: Classifier evasion asks how little an input must change before a classifier gives it a different prediction. This paper develops two systematic ways to find such changes for tree ensembles, including boosted trees and random forests. The goal is to identify nearby prediction-changing examples under specified constraints.

The first method formulates the search as a mixed integer linear program and uses a solver to find the optimal evading instance. It supports an expressive collection of constraints. The second method sacrifices optimality for speed through symbolic prediction, an algorithm for computing finite differences efficiently on tree ensembles. The two methods therefore provide different choices between solution quality and search cost.

On a digit-recognition task, both gradient boosted trees and random forests prove highly susceptible to evasion. The authors then strengthen a boosted tree model by adding evading examples to the training data at each boosting round. This adversarial boosting procedure hardens the evaluated model without reducing predictive accuracy, connecting systematic attack generation to a concrete training-based defense.
icml-2016-evasion-and-hardening-of-tree-.tldr: Two algorithms find evasions for tree ensembles, and adversarial boosting hardens an evaluated model without sacrificing predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies the expressive power of ReLU networks: which decision boundaries they can represent and how many hidden units that representation requires. It focuses on two-layer networks and compares them with threshold networks. This shifts attention from the practical training benefits of ReLUs to the size of networks needed to express equivalent decisions.

The authors construct threshold networks that reproduce the decision boundaries of two-layer ReLU networks. Although such a representation is possible, the threshold network may need exponentially more hidden units. The result identifies a potential representational efficiency advantage for ReLUs; it does not say that every equivalent threshold network must always incur that expansion.

The paper also gives sufficient conditions under which a sign network can be represented by a ReLU network with a corresponding logarithmic reduction in hidden units. Experiments compare threshold networks with their much smaller ReLU counterparts on synthetic data. Together, the theoretical constructions and empirical comparisons examine how compact representation relates to learning, while preserving the conditional nature of the size-reduction results.
icml-2016-expressiveness-of-rectifier-ne.tldr: Two-layer ReLU networks can represent decision boundaries whose equivalent threshold-network representations may require exponentially more hidden units.

paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to convex optimization: simulated annealing, which uses random walks, and interior-point methods that follow a central path. The authors show that simulated annealing is directly equivalent, in a particular sense, to central-path optimization using the entropic universal barrier. The connection provides a way to transfer ideas between these methods.

One consequence is a new temperature schedule for simulated annealing, motivated by how interior-point algorithms follow their central paths. Under the membership-oracle model, where access to a convex set is through tests of whether points belong to it, this schedule improves the state-of-the-art time complexity for convex optimization.

A second consequence is an efficient randomized interior-point method with an efficiently computable universal barrier for any convex set described by a membership oracle. Previously, efficiently computable barriers were available only for particular convex sets. The importance of the equivalence is therefore algorithmic: it yields both a faster annealing approach and a broader way to construct usable interior-point methods.
icml-2016-faster-convex-optimization-sim.tldr: A qualified equivalence between simulated annealing and interior-point methods yields faster convex optimization and an efficiently computable universal barrier.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires an agent to explore while using what it has learned to guide decisions. Generalization adds another requirement: experience should inform more than the individual situations already encountered. This paper proposes randomized least-squares value iteration, RLSVI, to address both requirements through value functions whose parameters enter linearly.

The authors explain why least-squares value iteration combined with Boltzmann or epsilon-greedy exploration can be highly inefficient. RLSVI instead places randomization in the value functions used to guide learning. Computational results demonstrate dramatic efficiency improvements, providing empirical support for this alternative way of coordinating value estimation and exploration.

The paper also proves an upper bound on expected regret that establishes near-optimality in a tabula rasa learning setting. That theoretical conclusion has a specific scope and should be distinguished from the broader ambition of combining exploration with generalization. Taken together, the computational results and regret analysis suggest that randomized value functions are a promising approach to this joint challenge, rather than establishing near-optimality in every setting with function approximation.
icml-2016-generalization-and-exploration.tldr: RLSVI uses randomized value functions for efficient exploration and generalization, with near-optimal regret established in a tabula rasa setting.

paragraphs: Metric learning asks how to choose a distance measure from data. This paper revisits learning a Euclidean metric and derives a simple optimization formulation from first principles. Its central computational feature is a closed-form solution, giving a direct way to obtain the learned metric from the formulation.

The solution also has a geometric interpretation through the Riemannian geometry of positive definite matrices. That connection gives the method mathematical structure alongside its computational simplicity. The authors emphasize interpretability as another attractive property, making the proposal a combination of a clear optimization problem, an interpretable solution, and a geometric account of that solution.

The reported computations are several orders of magnitude faster than the widely used LMNN and ITML methods. On standard benchmark datasets, the closed-form method also consistently achieves higher classification accuracy. These empirical findings suggest that the simpler formulation can improve both speed and predictive usefulness in the evaluated settings. The paper’s contribution is therefore broader than obtaining a convenient formula: it connects that formula to favorable practical metric-learning results.
icml-2016-geometric-mean-metric-learning.tldr: A closed-form metric-learning formulation combines geometric interpretability with reported speed and classification-accuracy gains over LMNN and ITML.

paragraphs: Column subset selection chooses a collection of columns from a data matrix, with feature selection as an important application. Greedy selection has worked well in practice, but its theoretical performance has been less fully understood, particularly when computation is distributed. This paper examines that gap through both analysis and experiments.

The authors improve the approximation guarantee for the greedy algorithm and show that their bound is tight up to a constant factor. This gives a more precise account of the quality that the method can guarantee. Tightness also indicates that the bound captures the relevant behavior closely, apart from a constant-factor difference.

The paper then presents the first distributed implementation with provable approximation factors. It uses randomized composable core-sets, an idea developed in work on submodular maximization, to support selection across distributed data. An empirical study validates the effectiveness of the resulting algorithm. The combined contribution strengthens the theoretical basis of a practical greedy method and extends it to a setting where the work is distributed.
icml-2016-greedy-column-subset-selection.tldr: The paper sharpens guarantees for greedy column selection and introduces a distributed implementation with provable approximation quality.

paragraphs: Log-linear probabilistic models are specified up to a normalization constant, and learning them typically requires many inference queries. When the output space is large, those queries can be intractable and dominate the cost of training. This paper addresses the repeated nature of that bottleneck by considering a sequence of related inference problems together.

The proposed approach amortizes inference cost using a connection to similarity-search algorithms for large databases. Through maximum inner product search, techniques developed for searching large collections become useful for probabilistic learning and inference. The central idea is to reduce the cumulative work associated with related queries, making the sequence itself an opportunity for computational savings.

The method achieves improved running times with provable approximation guarantees. Evaluations on synthetic data and neural language models with large output spaces show that it performs well in the tested settings. The contribution links faster approximate inference to the practical demands of learning, where an efficient answer to one query matters less than efficiently handling the many queries needed over training.
icml-2016-learning-and-inference-via-max.tldr: Maximum inner product search helps amortize related inference queries, accelerating log-linear model learning with approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Studying an evolving population is difficult when researchers can observe snapshots but cannot track the same individuals over time. Experimental cost or privacy can make individual trajectories unavailable. This paper asks whether those cross-sectional observations can reveal the stochastic process governing population dynamics, including processes involved in cell differentiation.

The authors show that recovery is possible within a class of processes even when samples come from only a few distinct times. They analyze different recoverability conditions and establish reversibility as a sufficient condition. This is a conditional recovery result: reversibility provides one route to recoverability, rather than being presented as a necessary requirement for every recoverable process.

For estimation, the paper derives a loss function and regularization and represents the processes as diffusive recurrent neural networks. The approach is demonstrated using existing biological assays to uncover complex cellular dynamics described as an epigenetic landscape. The contribution connects a theoretical account of what population snapshots can reveal with a trainable model for estimating those dynamics.
icml-2016-learning-population-level-diff.tldr: Diffusive recurrent networks estimate population dynamics from snapshots, with recovery guarantees for a class of processes and reversibility as a sufficient condition.

paragraphs: Kernel machines face substantial computation and storage costs on large datasets. Conjugate gradient methods help because they can operate without storing the entire kernel matrix and can take advantage of parallel computation. However, poorly conditioned kernel matrices can make their convergence slow, leaving an important obstacle even after storage demands are reduced.

This paper proposes preconditioned conjugate gradients for kernel machines and develops a broad collection of preconditioners suited to kernel matrices. Preconditioning addresses the numerical structure that makes the iterative solver struggle. The authors use this approach both to solve kernel-machine problems and to learn their hyperparameters, extending the computational strategy beyond a single fixed model fit.

The method is exact in the limit of iterations, so its accuracy claim is tied to continued iterative computation. For a fixed computational budget, the reported results outperform state-of-the-art approximations. The practical message is that improving the convergence of an iterative solver can make kernel methods competitive under limited resources while retaining an exact limiting solution.
icml-2016-preconditioning-kernel-matrice.tldr: Kernel-specific preconditioners accelerate conjugate-gradient learning, outperforming reported approximations at a fixed budget while remaining exact in the iteration limit.

paragraphs: Publishers selling advertising inventory can use low-regret learning algorithms to choose among ad exchanges. Their choices evolve as they learn which exchange offers favorable prices. This creates a pricing problem for an exchange: it must attract sellers and maximize revenue while interacting with counterparties whose decisions are themselves produced by learning algorithms.

The paper formulates this interaction as a learning problem and develops pricing algorithms for the exchange. Its central result is that knowing the seller uses a low-regret algorithm is enough for the exchange to obtain its own low-regret algorithm for finding the optimal price. The seller’s learning behavior supplies the key assumption supporting that result.

This matters because the pricing decision is linked to an adaptive counterparty, rather than treated as an isolated choice against fixed behavior. The result shows that a broad performance property of the seller’s algorithm can support a learning guarantee for the exchange as well. The stated conclusion remains conditional on low-regret behavior by the counterparty in the formulated problem.
icml-2016-pricing-a-low-regret-seller-eb.tldr: Knowing that sellers use low-regret learning is sufficient for an exchange to develop its own low-regret pricing algorithm.

paragraphs: Random embeddings can approximate kernel functions, but constructing and applying them also requires computation. This paper proposes reusing Gaussian random vectors within structured matrices to obtain sublinear-time kernel approximations. The framework includes Fastfood as a special case and extends to circulant, Toeplitz, Hankel, and the broader family of low-displacement-rank matrices.

The theoretical analysis introduces measures of coherence and graph-based structural constants that control approximation quality. It also proves unbiasedness and low-variance properties for random feature maps produced within the framework. These results address the statistical consequences of imposing structure and reusing randomness, alongside the computational benefits motivating the construction.

For low-displacement matrices, the amount of structure and randomness can be adjusted. Reducing statistical variance comes at the cost of more computation and storage, giving an explicit tradeoff rather than a uniform improvement on every dimension. Empirical findings strongly support the theory and the use of a wider range of structured matrices to scale kernel methods through random features.
icml-2016-recycling-randomness-with-stru.tldr: Reusing Gaussian randomness in structured matrices enables fast kernel approximations with theoretical quality guarantees and adjustable variance–computation tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Drawing a discrete random sample is a basic operation in Monte Carlo methods, but that operation can become expensive in large inference problems. The difficulty considered here arises when a discrete variable has many dependencies, as commonly occurs in large Bayesian models and graphical models. The paper seeks to reduce the computation needed for this sampling step.

The authors propose an approximate solution based on subsampling and connect discrete sampling to multi-armed bandit problems with finite reward populations. This connection provides the foundation for three algorithms with theoretical guarantees. It turns tools for a different sequential decision problem into a way to design computationally efficient sampling procedures.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world large-scale problems show that the approximate algorithms are robust and efficient. The approximation is an explicit part of the contribution, alongside the supporting guarantees. The significance is that a frequently repeated building block of inference can be approached through selective computation, with both analysis and empirical evidence supporting the resulting sampling methods.
icml-2016-scalable-discrete-sampling-as-.tldr: A connection to finite-population bandit problems yields three theoretically supported subsampling algorithms for efficient approximate discrete sampling.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression in which an observation is a nonlinear function of a weighted combination of input features, plus noise. The unknown parameter vector is sparse, meaning only a limited set of its entries is nonzero. The goal is to recover that vector despite the nonlinear relationship between inputs and observations.

The authors propose least squares with an l1 penalty to encourage sparsity. Because the prediction passes through a nonlinear function, the resulting optimization problem is nonconvex. This creates a distinction between finding a globally optimal objective value and obtaining a statistically accurate estimate of the underlying parameters.

The main theorem shows that, under mild conditions, every stationary point of the objective achieves an optimal statistical convergence rate. The guarantee concerns estimation accuracy under those conditions; it does not assert that the objective becomes convex. Numerical results support the theoretical analysis. The contribution explains how nonconvex optimization can still yield statistically strong parameter estimates in this sparse nonlinear regression setting.
icml-2016-sparse-nonlinear-regression-pa.tldr: Under mild conditions, every stationary point of an l1-regularized sparse nonlinear regression objective attains an optimal statistical convergence rate.

paragraphs: Distance calculations are central to clustering, and reducing their cost can make large problems more manageable. This paper introduces a way to approximate Euclidean distances using block vectors together with the Hölder inequality. The approximation supplies lower bounds that can be used to accelerate clustering while preserving the quality of the result.

The role of the bounds is important: the method uses an approximation to support computational shortcuts without requiring a loss in clustering quality. This connects a mathematical inequality to the practical work of distance evaluation. The paper applies that idea to a clustering algorithm intended to reduce the computational burden of k-means.

Extensive experiments report substantial reductions in computing time compared with standard methods and Yinyang k-means. The authors also show that the presented algorithm’s memory consumption does not depend on the number of clusters, a property they identify as useful for large-scale problems. Together, the timing results and memory claim support the method as an efficient way to carry out clustering.
icml-2016-speeding-up-k-means-by-approxi.tldr: Block-vector distance bounds accelerate k-means without loss of clustering quality and provide memory consumption independent of the number of clusters.

paragraphs: Square Root Graphical Models extend single-variable exponential-family distributions into models of several interacting variables. The motivation is a restriction in earlier exponential and Poisson graphical models: they could not represent positive dependencies. Such dependencies matter in applications, including the tendency for airport delays in different cities to increase together.

The proposed exponential generalization supports almost arbitrary positive and negative dependencies, subject to a mild condition on its parameter matrix resembling the positive-definiteness condition for a Gaussian covariance matrix. The Poisson generalization permits both dependency signs without constraints on parameter values. These are distinct results, with a matrix condition retained for the exponential case.

The authors develop parameter estimation through node-wise regressions with l1 regularization and approximate likelihood calculations using sampling. They demonstrate the exponential model on synthetic data and real airport delay data. The contribution expands the dependency patterns available to these distribution families and supplies estimation tools, making the additional modeling flexibility usable in the evaluated settings.
icml-2016-square-root-graphical-models-m.tldr: Square Root Graphical Models allow positive and negative dependencies in exponential and Poisson generalizations, with corresponding estimation methods.
